followUps:
I cut anything that does not change the core design, and I say it out loud so the interviewer can disagree. I ask what the main user action is, then list features as must, nice, or skip. For a news feed, posting, editing and ads are usually out; loading, scrolling and liking stay in.

I confirm the list in one sentence ('I will skip auth and the backend; OK?'). That turns a guess into an agreement and saves time later.

I shorten the requirements and the final optimisation sweep, never the data model or the interface. State shape and the API contract are what the interviewer grades most, and mistakes there are expensive to fix later.

With 45 minutes, a rough split is 5 for requirements, 10 for architecture, 15 for data and API, 10 for the one or two deep dives, and 5 for the rest. I list the skipped topics at the end ('next I would cover accessibility and error states') so the gap is visible and deliberate.

code.title: Autocomplete: drop stale replies with a stamp

followUps:
Debounce waits until typing pauses, then searches once; throttle searches at a steady rate while typing continues. For autocomplete I use debounce, because only the final text matters.

Example: typing 'react' in 400 ms with a 200 ms debounce sends one request for 'react'. A 200 ms throttle would send about two requests for 'r' and 'rea', both quickly out of date. Throttle suits continuous events such as scroll or drag. Cost is one timer, O(1). Always keep the input itself un-debounced.

Do not search while the user is mid-composition, because the text is not final yet. Listen to compositionstart and compositionend and keep a flag.

let composing = false;
input.oncompositionstart = () => composing = true;
input.oncompositionend = () => { composing = false; schedule(input.value); };
input.oninput = () => { if (!composing) schedule(input.value); };

Without this, typing Japanese or Chinese sends requests for half-typed syllables like 'n' and 'ni' before the character is chosen.

429 means 'too many requests', so stop sending and wait, do not retry at once. Read the Retry-After header if present, otherwise back off exponentially with jitter (for example 1 s, 2 s, 4 s).

Meanwhile keep the previous suggestions on screen, show a small 'try again shortly' message, and serve repeated queries from the cache. Also raise the debounce time and the minimum length so fewer requests go out. Never show an empty list as if there were no matches.

code.title: Offset vs cursor pagination with an insert

followUps:
With a ranked feed there is no stable 'created before' order, so the cursor must encode the ranking position and a snapshot, not just a time. The server keeps a ranked list per session (or a signed token holding score and id) and returns the next slice from it.

Items may move up or down between requests, so some repeats or gaps are still possible. The server fixes this by freezing the ranked list for the session, or the client de-duplicates by id. Fresh posts are shown through a 'new posts' button instead of changing the list under the reader.

De-duplicate by id when appending: keep a Set of ids already shown and skip any that are in it.

const seen = new Set(items.map(i => i.id));
const fresh = page.items.filter(i => !seen.has(i.id));
items = items.concat(fresh);
cursor = page.nextCursor;

Example: items 10 9 8 7 shown, next page returns 7 6 5 4, the 7 is dropped. Cost O(page size) time, O(total items) memory for the set. Store items in a map by id so updates replace instead of duplicate.

code.title: Virtualization: compute the visible window

followUps:
Keep a cumulative (prefix sum) array of heights and binary search it. If row heights are 30, 50, 40, the offsets are 0, 30, 80, 120. To find the row at scrollTop 85, binary search for the last offset not above 85, which is row 2.

Unknown heights start as an estimate, and after a row renders you measure it (ResizeObserver) and update the sums from that row on. Lookup is O(log N); an update is O(N) in the worst case, or O(log N) with a Fenwick tree. Adjust scrollTop if rows above the viewport change size, or the list jumps.

content-visibility: auto is a CSS hint that lets the browser skip layout and painting for off-screen elements, while they stay in the DOM. It is enough for a few thousand mostly static sections, because find-in-page, anchors and accessibility keep working.

It is not enough for tens of thousands of rows: all nodes still exist, so memory and style cost grow with N. Pair it with contain-intrinsic-size so the scrollbar does not jump. Use it first when it is good enough, and virtualise only when profiling says so.

code.title: Optimistic like with rollback

followUps:
I use a library in the same cache pattern: onMutate saves and changes the cache, onError restores it, onSettled refetches the truth.

onMutate: async () => {
  await qc.cancelQueries({queryKey});
  const prev = qc.getQueryData(queryKey);
  qc.setQueryData(queryKey, next);
  return { prev };
},
onError: (e, v, ctx) => qc.setQueryData(queryKey, ctx.prev),
onSettled: () => qc.invalidateQueries({queryKey})

Cancelling queries first stops an in-flight refetch overwriting the optimistic value.

PUT and DELETE are idempotent, so repeating them gives the same result. A toggle endpoint flips state each time, so a retry after a timeout can undo the like.

Example: the user likes, the request succeeds but the response is lost, the client retries. PUT /posts/7/like again leaves 'liked'. A toggle would now show 'unliked' on the server and 'liked' on screen. The client sends the desired state, not a flip, so the server and UI always agree, and retries are safe.

Use translateX when slides must be animated as a strip with custom easing, when you need an infinite loop, or when scroll-snap behaves differently across browsers. You move one track element with transform: translateX(-index * 100%) and a CSS transition.

The cost: you lose native touch momentum and keyboard scrolling, so you must write swipe handling with pointer events and keep off-screen slides inert for accessibility. Transforms run on the GPU and do not cause layout, so animation stays smooth. Scroll-snap remains my default for simple carousels.

Clone the first and last slides at the opposite ends, then jump silently after the animation finishes. With slides A B C, the track is C' A B C A'. Moving past C slides to A'; on transitionend you disable the transition, set the position to the real A, and re-enable it on the next frame.

The user sees nothing because A' and A look identical. Edge cases: fast repeated clicks (ignore input during a move) and screen readers (hide clones with aria-hidden and inert so duplicates are not announced).

code.title: Ordered, de-duplicated delivery by sequence number

followUps:
The server's sequence number is the real order; a timestamp is not, because client clocks differ and two messages can share the same millisecond. A phone that is two minutes fast would put its messages in the wrong place forever.

Example: A sends at 10:00:05 by a fast clock, B replies at 10:00:03 by a slow clock. Sorting by time shows B's reply before the question. A sequence number assigned by one server per conversation is a total order with no ties. Timestamps are fine for display only.

Do not replay thousands one by one; load a fresh snapshot instead. If the gap is bigger than a limit (say 200), drop the local buffer, fetch the latest page over REST, and show history on scroll upward.

Steps: 1) detect serverLastSeq - lastSeq > limit; 2) fetch the newest 50 messages; 3) set lastSeq to the newest; 4) mark older ones as 'load more'. Small gaps use afterSeq ranges in pages. This keeps the reconnect time constant instead of growing with the time offline.

Use one connection per browser, owned by a single tab, and share it with the others. A SharedWorker can hold the socket and message all tabs; where it is not supported, elect a leader tab with the Web Locks API or BroadcastChannel, and the leader forwards messages.

Why: ten tabs with ten sockets waste server connections and show duplicate notifications. The leader holds the socket; if it closes, the lock is released and another tab takes over, resuming from the saved lastSeq.

code.title: Unread count from two numbers

followUps:
Mark as read only when the user can really see the newest message: the tab is visible and focused, the conversation is open, and the last message is on screen (IntersectionObserver). Opening the app in a background tab should not clear the badge.

Send the receipt with a short delay (about 500 ms) and batch it as upToSeq. Example: lastSeq 120, lastReadSeq 100; after the user scrolls to the bottom you send 120 and unread becomes 0. Use a max rule on the server so an old receipt cannot move the marker backwards.

For a group, store one lastReadSeq per member, not a row per message per person. A message is read by a member if its seq is at most that member's marker.

Example: members have markers 10, 14, 20; message 12 was read by two of the three. A row per message and member would cost N times M rows, while markers cost M numbers per conversation. For big groups show just 'seen by 2' counts or hide receipts, and update them lazily, since sending a receipt to everyone is expensive.

code.title: Reconnect back-off with jitter

followUps:
If the counter resets as soon as the socket opens, a server that accepts then immediately closes the connection (overloaded or rejecting the token) makes every client retry after 1 second, forever, which can overload it further.

Waiting until the connection has lasted, say, 10 seconds proves it is healthy. Example: attempts go 1 s, 2 s, 4 s; at attempt 3 the socket opens but dies after 1 s, so the counter stays and the next wait is 8 s, not 1 s. This keeps back-off growing during a flapping outage.

Show a clear but calm status: a banner such as 'Offline, reconnecting...' based on navigator.onLine and the socket state, and keep the app usable. Show previously loaded data, mark queued messages with a clock icon, and disable only actions that truly need the server.

When the connection returns, remove the banner, flush the outbox, and mark messages as sent. If it stays down for a long time, show a 'Retry now' button. Never block the whole screen or discard the user's draft.

code.title: Spreadsheet recalculation with Kahn order

followUps:
Do not loop over a million cells on each change; keep an aggregate that updates by the difference. For SUM, store the running total, and when one cell changes from 5 to 8 add 3. That is O(1) per edit instead of O(N).

Range nodes make this work: one node 'A1:A1000000' has the precedent cells as inputs and a cached sum. For MIN, MAX or other non-invertible functions, use a segment tree: update in O(log N), query in O(log N). The first full calculation is still O(N), done lazily in chunks so the UI does not freeze.

Cells at the same dependency level do not depend on each other, so they can be computed in parallel. Group the topological order into levels: level 0 has no dirty precedents, level 1 depends only on level 0, and so on. Send each level to Web Workers and wait before the next.

Example: A1 is level 0; B1 and C1 (both read A1 only) are level 1 and run together. The gain only appears for wide graphs with expensive formulas, because passing data to workers costs time. For typical sheets a single thread is faster, so measure first.

Edits become small operations (set cell A1 to 5) instead of whole-sheet saves, and the server orders them. Two users editing different cells merge trivially; the same cell uses last-writer-wins by server order, or a CRDT for text-like content.

Each client recalculates locally from the operations, so only raw inputs are shared, not computed values, and every client reaches the same result if operations are applied in the same order. Cursors and selections are sent separately as light presence data. Cycles created by two concurrent edits are caught by the same cycle check on every client.

code.title: Grid column offsets with binary search

followUps:
Keep an array of column widths and a prefix-sum offsets array. When one width changes, only offsets from that column onward change, so recompute from that index to the end.

Example: widths 80, 120, 60 give offsets 0, 80, 200, 260. Widen column 1 to 220: the offsets become 0, 80, 300, 360. During a drag, update a CSS variable or transform for the visible columns in requestAnimationFrame, and commit the full recompute on pointer up. Cost is O(columns) per resize, still tiny for a few thousand columns.

Put headers in a separate element outside the scrolling body and drive its position from the body's scroll position. Listen to scroll on the body and set the header's transform: translateX(-scrollLeft) in the same animation frame.

Alternatives: position: sticky for the header row and first column, which the browser keeps aligned with no JavaScript, or a single scroll container with sticky headers. Sticky is simplest and avoids drift; use the transform approach only when headers live in a different layer, such as canvas.

I cut polish first and keep the working core. The order is: nice-to-have features, animations and styling, then secondary edge cases. I never cut the main flow, keyboard support for the basic action, or empty and error states for it.

I tell the interviewer what I am dropping and why ('I will skip drag animation and use a plain move; I would add it with more time'). A small working app with a clear list of next steps scores higher than a large one that is broken.

I use it openly and sparingly, if the rules allow, and I check the rules first. Good uses: boilerplate, mock data, a list of edge cases, a quick review. I keep ownership of the state shape, the component split and the trade-offs.

I ask for small pieces, read every line, and run it right away. I will not paste code I cannot explain, because the interviewer will ask me to change it live. I say aloud what I asked and why, and fix any weakness I find, such as a missing cleanup or request cancellation.

code.title: Kanban moveCard pure function

followUps:
Store a sortable position key on each card instead of an index, so moving one card changes only that card. Fractional indexing gives a card between positions 1.0 and 2.0 the key 1.5; the next between 1.0 and 1.5 gets 1.25.

The server sorts by key within a column. Example: cards a=1, b=2, c=3; move c between a and b and set c=1.5, one write, where an integer index would rewrite b and c. Keys grow longer after many inserts, so use string keys (like 'a0', 'a0V') and rebalance the column occasionally.

The last write wins on the card's column and position, unless the server detects the conflict. The simplest safe design sends moves as operations with the card's version number; if the version is stale, the server rejects it and returns the current board.

Example: user A moves card 5 to Done, user B moves it to Doing a second later. The server applies A, then B (last writer wins), and broadcasts both, so every client ends in Doing. The client that lost sees the card jump, so show a brief highlight and a live-region message. Moves of different cards never conflict.

I make the board a pure function and test it with a handful of inputs before drawing anything. For a Kanban board, moveCard(board, id, to, index) is checked on small boards, and the UI is checked by hand.

Fast checks: 1) run the code and try normal use; 2) try edges (empty list, one item, drop in place, rapid clicks); 3) search for known mistakes (no cleanup, offset paging, innerHTML, mouse-only); 4) add three quick asserts. Reading takes minutes; a hidden bug found by the interviewer costs far more.

I would not delegate the requirements, the state model, the API contract or the final decision on trade-offs, because those are the thinking being graded. I also would not hand over security-sensitive code (auth, escaping user input) without reading it line by line.

I delegate typing, not judgement. Example: I define the board as column id to array of card ids, then ask for the CSS grid. If I cannot explain a function to the interviewer in a sentence, I rewrite it myself.
